Threat.value: I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
The world is a dangerous place

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'explosion or bang sounds' is a poor fit unless there was a firearm discharge or similar blast-like cue; nothing else in the profile suggests that context, so this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'I have lost my connection to my community and culture' is difficult to justify from the rest of this profile for an adult European married teacher after a mugging/robbery. The other appraisals focus on self-blame/institutional failure, but this item implies a broader cultural/community rupture that is not supported by the trauma type, demographics, or other nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, the profile otherwise centers on external danger, sensory reliving, and mistrust/injustice. 'Violated Values' implies the patient did something morally incongruent during the event, but there are no accompanying memory, threat, trigger, or strategy items suggesting perpetration, betrayal of others, failure to act, or shame-based self-condemnation. In this profile it stands apart from the rest of the formulation and is the least clinically coherent item.

vignette: Elias Vance stood by his locked car door in the staff parking lot when a silver sedan squealed to a halt beside him. Two men had jumped out, their hands already inside his jacket before he could react. The lead attacker shouted, the sound sharp and metallic like a dropped wrench against the asphalt, and when Elias raised his hands, he caught the cold, copper taste of blood and cheap tobacco in his mouth. They grabbed his wallet and phone, then melted back into the night. For weeks afterward, Elias told himself it was a statistical aberration, but the incident had fractured his baseline. When he walked through the crowded faculty lounge the following Tuesday, the press of bodies against his shoulders instantly pulled the parking lot back to the forefront of his awareness, the taste of copper flooding his mouth before he could stop it. The suddenness of the violation, combined with the fact that campus security had dismissed his report as an overreaction, cemented a quiet certainty in him: the world had become an unshielded space where institutions abandoned their own to fend for themselves. As the months bled into the following semester, the habit of hyper-vigilance hardened into routine. Driving to work with his wife in the passenger seat became a source of quiet dread; the mere presence of another driver’s erratic lane change or the sudden blare of a car horn would trigger a visceral jolt, as if his body were still bracing for the sedan beside him. His threat monitoring never switched off. He found himself studying the faces of his students and colleagues, looking for the telltale shift in posture or narrowed eyes that signaled hostile intent, and he was certain that scanning the room for exits before he even sat down at his desk kept him safe. Yet the more he scanned, the more the memories intruded. When a classroom projector suddenly whirred to life or a desk chair scraped against the floor, the uncontrolled access of the memory would force its way into his mind, the sensory reliving so complete that he could feel the gravel of the parking lot through his shoes again. Every time the memory forced its way into his mind, the sensory vividness reinforced his conviction that what happened was deeply unfair and that the world remained a hostile place. By the time spring arrived, the cycle had tightened around his life until he could barely breathe through it. The belief that the injustice of that mugging had gone unaddressed now dictated his choices, pushing him to avoid staff meetings where large groups gathered or to leave early if a colleague’s sudden movement made him flinch. Each avoidance, however, only deepened the conviction that the world was fundamentally unsafe, which in turn made the memories return with greater force. He would be grading papers in his study when a distant siren or the heavy tread of footsteps on his porch would pull the past back, the uncontrolled intrusion meaning that ordinary sounds now carried the same paralyzing weight as that October night, stretching his sensitivity to crowds and sudden movements beyond endurance. The constant scanning for exits and reading of hostile cues only confirmed his belief that the institutions meant to keep him safe had failed, leaving him alone in a dangerous environment, while his body’s reflexive bracing to every movement made him shrink further from the very spaces he once taught in. His wife noticed the distance in his eyes, the way he would tense when she reached across the table to touch his hand, but what kept him from speaking up was the fear that acknowledging the breakdown would confirm his worst suspicion: that no one was coming to fix what had been broken. When he finally scheduled an appointment with a clinician, it was not because the pain had faded, but because the exhaustion of living in a permanently active alert state had finally outpaced his ability to hide it. He hoped, more than anything, to find a way to turn off the alarm, to trust that the parking lot would stay empty, and to walk through a crowded room without tasting copper.
